name: PT ESSA Industries Indonesia Tbk.

frontmatter.title: ESSA Industries: ammonia at the bottom of the global cost curve, priced for a collapse
frontmatter.summary: ESSA runs one ammonia train in Central Sulawesi, sells all of it to an affiliated trader at a published index, buys gas on a long contract and carries net cash. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp941: the shares price a collapse in ammonia revenue that the contracted cost base does not justify. The dividend and the cash pile set the floor; the ammonia cycle sets the return.
thesis: One train, one offtaker, one gas field: the Luwuk ammonia plant sells its entire output to Genesis at Fertecon index and buys Senoro feedstock under the gas sales agreement signed in October 2026, a cost position most European capacity no longer has [S2, S8, S9].
The market is short a crash it may not get: at Rp496 the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of -19.9%, deeper than our -10.0% base case [S0].
2026 is already earned: nine-month revenue US$310.9m and attributable profit US$51.1m after a major turnaround, with realised ammonia at US$531/t in the first half [S3, S4].

The balance sheet is the floor: at the FY2025 year-end the company held US$125.8m of cash against US$0.2m of debt, capex was guided at US$10.0m to US$20.0m, and a dividend was already paid at Rp52.0/share [S0, S7, S6].
We hold gross margin between the FY2023 margin trough and the FY2022 spike and still find value, because the DCF is run on the mid-cycle rather than on the 2026 spike [S2].

catalysts.event: Tampa ammonia settlement for December, the first test of whether the autumn price spike holds
Senoro-Toili volumes flowing under the sales agreement signed in late October 2026
FY2026 audited results: realised ammonia price, dividend declaration and capex guidance into the next turnaround cycle
European gas into the following winter and the size of the curtailment it forces on regional ammonia capacity

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT ESSA Industries Indonesia at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp941, 89.8% above the Rp496 price and 103.2% total return once the Rp66 of dividends we expect over the next twelve months is added. The target is the probability-weighted average of three scenario values — Rp442 on a faster ammonia normalisation, Rp823 on our most likely path and Rp1,678 if European curtailment persists — rolled forward a year at the cost of equity and net of the interim dividend.

The company is a single-asset ammonia producer. One train at Luwuk in Central Sulawesi, running on Senoro-Toili gas, sells its whole output to an affiliated trading house at the Fertecon index [S2]. That structure removes almost every commercial variable except the ammonia price itself: the feedstock is contracted, the offtake is contracted, the product is a globally traded commodity and the balance sheet carries no debt [S2, S9].

The argument for owning it here is not that ammonia stays where it is. It is that the share price has already discounted a fall deeper than the one we forecast. At Rp496 the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of -19.9% against our -10.0%, with the shortfall applied to revenue growth in every forecast year rather than as a single bad year — a collapse in the ammonia price carried through the whole forecast, on top of a volume base whose only interruption in 2026 was a planned turnaround [S0, S2, S3]. On our most likely path the shares are worth Rp823 a year out before the dividend, and the bear case at Rp442 is below today's price before the payout and only just above it once it is added.

Three things move the value. The first is the ammonia price, which is set by the European gas complex rather than by anything ESSA does: industry estimates put the curtailed share at about a third of European ammonia production capacity, and Tampa settled at US$645/t for November [S8]. The second is the cost of the Senoro feedstock, reset by a sales agreement signed on 28 October 2026 covering 205.59 BSCF; neither the term nor the price formula is disclosed, and at the plant's disclosed gas intake that volume covers roughly the explicit forecast window, so we assume an oil-linked cost through the forecast and a market price at renewal [S9, S2]. The third is capital allocation: on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the company carries net cash equal to a large fraction of the Rp496 share price, holds no debt, and guides protection capex at only US$10.0m to US$20.0m, so the plant converts every dollar of margin into distributable cash, and the board has demonstrated it will pay it out [S0, S7, S6].

The two cross-checks sit well below the DCF, at Rp599 and Rp339, and we explain in the valuation section why that is a low-point earnings artefact rather than a second opinion. The main risk is not the balance sheet but a supply cycle that turns faster than we assume; the scenario table further down sizes that.

The ex-cash arithmetic is the strongest bull argument and deserves stating plainly. The 30 June 2026 balance sheet carries net cash equal to a large fraction of a Rp496 share price [S0]. With net cash netted off, the enterprise itself trades at 2.5x FY2026E EBITDA and 2.8x the following year, with a free cash flow to equity yield of 23.7% and a dividend yield of 13.4% [S0, S6]. Buying ESSA at today's price is buying the ammonia plant at a trough multiple and getting the cash pile and the payout for little more than book. What the market appears to be pricing is the dividend — at these yields the share is held for the distribution and the cash pile, not for growth — which is why a payout cut or a project decision that traps the cash is the fastest way to lose the floor.

ESSA is an Indonesian ammonia and LPG producer whose operating substance sits almost entirely in one subsidiary. PT Panca Amara Utama owns the ammonia train at Luwuk in Banggai, Central Sulawesi, held through PT ESSA Chemicals Indonesia and consolidated at just under seventy per cent ownership, with the remaining thirty per cent in non-controlling hands [S2]. The group also owns a smaller LPG and condensate plant at Palembang in South Sumatra and small project vehicles for sustainable aviation fuel and blue ammonia, but the ammonia business dominates: ammonia revenue was US$255.4m of US$295.0m of group revenue in FY2025 [S2, F26, F1].

The ammonia plant is a single train built around KBR's Reforming Exchanger System and Purifier technology, with nameplate capacity of 700,000 MT/yr [S2]. It produced 748,274 MT of ammonia in FY2025 and sold 756,368 MT, the gap being an inventory draw rather than new capacity [S2, F17, F19]. Utilisation on the nameplate measure is above one hundred per cent, which is what debottlenecking looks like: the nameplate is a contractual and historic benchmark rather than the train's demonstrated throughput, and management has repeatedly guided to operational efficiency rather than new tonnage [S2, S7]. The June 2026 turnaround is the counterweight — more than a month down, and H1 volume fell even as the realised price rose — so the volume base is reliable across a year, not across a quarter [S3].

The commercial model is unusually simple. The entire ammonia output is sold to Genesis Corporation, a related party, at a price set by reference to Fertecon assessments in US dollars per tonne [S2]. That is not a cost-plus contract and it does not insulate the company from the cycle — it insulates it from marketing and credit risk while leaving the price exposure fully intact. The consequence is visible in the revenue series: there is one customer, and the price that customer pays is referenced to the international benchmark rather than set by ESSA [S2, F26]. The annual report is careful here: related-party terms are "mutually agreed upon" and "may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties", while the board states its belief that they are arm's length [S2]. Trade receivables confirm the concentration, with the Genesis balance US$24.7m of US$31.0m of trade receivables, and we treat the benchmark reference as disclosed rather than proven arm's length [S2, F47, F49].

The second business is small but not incidental. The Palembang plant produces LPG and condensate, with capacity now at 174 t/day of LPG after an expansion, and it generated US$36.1m of revenue on 64,811 MT of LPG sales in FY2025 [S2, F22, F23, F28]. LPG is a domestic, rupiah-linked business with a different margin structure from ammonia; it is the reason the group is not a pure single-commodity exposure, and it is the part of the company the ammonia minority does not own.

Strategy is deliberately narrow. Management describes capital spending as protection and maintenance rather than growth, guided the 2026 programme at US$10.0m to US$20.0m, and stated that new projects remain at an early stage with little capital required this year [S7, F38, F39]. The two options that could change the shape of the company — a blue-ammonia conversion of the existing train and a sustainable aviation fuel plant — are both pre-final-investment-decision. The SAF project was put on hold on 27 July 2026 with no material financial impact disclosed [S5], and the blue-ammonia study is at the reservoir and subsurface stage [S2]. Management has said it would look at methanol, hydrogen and urea if the economics justified it, which tells you more about optionality than about the plan [S7].

The company employs 487 people at group level [S0]. That is a small headcount for a plant of this size and reflects the contracted operating model: the plant is run under a management agreement with an affiliate, and the management fee of US$8.9m in FY2025 is the price of that arrangement [S2, F25].

Ammonia is one of the most widely traded industrial chemicals, and its cost of production is dominated
almost entirely by the price of the natural gas used as both feedstock and fuel. Plants with cheap
contracted gas sit at the bottom of the global cost curve; plants buying at hub prices sit at the top
and are the first to shut when gas is expensive. Because ammonia is expensive to store and costly to
ship relative to its value, the market clears regionally most of the time and only globally when price
gaps are wide. That structure is why European energy prices, rather than Asian demand, usually set the
marginal cost that producers elsewhere are paid against.

The ammonia market in late 2026 is being driven by a European supply shock rather than by Asian demand growth. European natural gas has moved above the level at which a large share of the region's ammonia capacity cannot cover its cash cost, and industry estimates put the curtailed share at roughly a third of regional capacity [S8]. The result is a firm price deck across every reference point that matters to ESSA: the Tampa November contract settled at US$645/t, up sharply on the prior month, Northwest European cargoes are quoted at US$730/t and Chinese export material at US$535/t [S8, F41, F42, F43]. Indian buyers are resisting above US$520/t, which caps how far the Asian price can run without European pull [S8, F50].

That is the mechanism that sets ESSA's revenue. The company sells at a Fertecon assessment, so its realised price is a lagged function of the same benchmark that Tampa and Northwest Europe are settling against [S2, S8]. The realised price in the first half of 2026 was US$531/t, up seventy per cent on the prior year, which is what happens when a marginal European producer's gas cost becomes the reference for a Sulawesi plant buying from a domestic field [S3].

The cost side is where ESSA differs from its listed peers. Raw materials used — the Senoro gas feedstock — were US$116.3m of US$196.2m of cost of revenues in FY2025, so feedstock is the majority of the cost base and everything else is largely fixed [S2, F24]. The gas is bought from the Senoro-Toili working area under a sales agreement; the KKKS consortium of Pertamina Hulu Energi Tomori Sulawesi, Medco E&P Tomori and Tomori E&P signed a new agreement with PAU on 28 October 2026 covering 205.59 BSCF [S9, F27]. The term is not stated in the article that carries the volume: at the plant's disclosed gas intake, 205.59 BSCF is about a decade of full-rate supply, so the volume — not a headline term — is what we model, and it roughly covers the explicit forecast [S9, S2, F27]. Indonesian upstream gas is sold on formulas linked to oil rather than to spot gas hubs, which is why our model carries the feedstock through Brent: the sector deck has Brent at US$96.0/bbl in 2026 and US$84.0/bbl in 2027, and we pass 65.0% of any move through to the selling price with 59.0% of the cost base exposed [S2, S9]. We could not source the contract's price formula, so the link is a calibration on the observed margin path rather than a contract reading.

Demand is the least interesting variable. Management puts traditional fertiliser-driven ammonia demand growth at a low single-digit rate per year, with no new capacity of its own before a blue-ammonia investment decision [S7]. The growth optionality sits in low-carbon applications — Japanese and Korean utilities co-firing ammonia in coal plants, and European carbon border pricing pushing buyers toward lower-footprint product — and management explicitly frames the blue-ammonia project as a way to qualify for those markets rather than as a volume play [S7, S2].

Competitive positioning is narrow but defensible. The Luwuk plant has three advantages that are hard to replicate: contracted low-cost gas from a dedicated field, a coastal site in eastern Indonesia close to Asian and Australian markets, and an offtake arrangement that removes working-capital and counterparty risk from the sales function [S2, S9]. Against that it has three weaknesses: it is a single train, so one outage removes all of the ammonia cash flow; it sells at a published index, so it has no pricing power at all; and its sole customer and its plant manager are both related parties, which concentrates governance risk in a small number of hands [S2, F26]. The feedstock supplier is not one of them: the gas comes from the Senoro-Toili KKKS joint operating body, an upstream consortium in which ESSA holds no interest [S2, S9].

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and contractual — the gas field consortium is the economic landlord. Buyer power is formally low but economically high, because the buyer pays an index and the index moves with the global cycle. New entrants are constrained by gas availability rather than by capital, which is why the supply threat comes from the Middle East and North America rather than from Indonesia. Substitution is a slow threat from low-carbon ammonia and, in fertiliser, from urea and phosphate choices that avoid ammonia altogether [S8]. Rivalry is global and commodity-like, with the European cost curve acting as the swing producer.

Indonesia has long used domestic gas allocation rules to keep feedstock available to fertiliser and
chemical producers at prices below export parity, and the country's ammonia industry was built on that
basis. That policy setting is the reason a plant in Central Sulawesi can compete with producers in the
Middle East and North America, and it is also the reason the industry's economics are so sensitive to
government decisions about which fields supply which plants at what formula.

The revenue history is an ammonia price series with a plant attached. Revenue fell from US$731.5m in FY2022 — the year of the European energy shock — to US$301.4m in FY2024 and US$295.0m in FY2025, a fall of more than half from the peak as the prior cycle unwound [S0]. Gross margin followed exactly the same path, from 46.6% at the top to 29.9% in FY2023 and 33.5% in FY2025 [S0]. Two caveats on that series: the pre-2023 lines are vendor data, because the FY2025 annual report carries only FY2023 to FY2025 [S2, S0]; and FY2023, not FY2025, was the margin trough at 29.9%, so the cycle low is below the year we use as the calibration anchor [S2, S0]. Volume barely moved through the whole period: the plant produced 748,274 MT of ammonia in FY2025 against a nameplate of 700,000 MT/yr, so almost every change in the financials is price [S2, F17, F27].

FY2025 was the bottom of the revenue cycle, though not of the margin. Revenue of US$295.0m, cost of revenues of US$196.2m, gross profit of US$98.9m, operating expenses of US$28.3m and an EBITDA of US$117.3m, an EBITDA margin of 39.8% [S2]. Net profit was US$55.1m, of which US$14.8m went to non-controlling interests and US$40.3m to shareholders, leaving a return on equity of 8.1% on US$583.6m of book equity, of which US$137.0m is the minority's share [S2, F15]. Tax was US$15.5m on pre-tax profit of US$70.6m, an effective rate consistent with the statutory rate [S2].

There is an earnings-quality flag that any reader of the vendor data needs to know about. The data pack carried a depreciation charge for FY2025 that was an order of magnitude below the audited figure of US$46.6m, and the same for FY2024 at US$46.4m [S2, F11, F12]. We restated both years from the segment note, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA from the vendor's implied figure to US$117.3m and the margin to 39.8%. The corroboration is the company's own half-year disclosure of US$73.0m of EBITDA on US$186.0m of revenue [S3], a margin consistent with the restated annual figure and not with one built on a token depreciation charge. One caveat we cannot close: FY2022 and FY2023 are not restated, because the FY2025 annual report presents only two comparative years, so the EBITDA lines for those years in the table below are understated by roughly the size of the depreciation charge shown for later periods [S2, F11].

The earnings-quality screen flags one item and we run it here rather than leaving it to the reader. Trade receivables rose to US$31.0m from US$21.5m while revenue fell, and the related-party Genesis balance rose to US$24.7m — four-fifths of the total [S2, F47, F48, F49]. Receivables growing faster than revenue is the classic divergence flag, and on FY2025 revenue the closing balance is about five weeks of sales, which is not a stretched DSO in absolute terms but is a sharp step up in a year when the top line shrank. Two explanations fit, and the filing does not let us choose between them: the fourth quarter carried higher-priced tonnage that had shipped but not settled at year-end, or the affiliate buyer was given longer terms as the ammonia price fell. We treat it as a timing effect in the base case because the June 2026 balance sheet shows payables and working capital reversing, but we have not been able to rule out a credit concession to the related party, and that is the reason the related-party section below carries a governance discount rather than a clean bill [S2, S0].

The cost base is simple and that is a virtue in a commodity business. Feedstock is US$116.3m of the US$196.2m cost of revenues, manufacturing expenses carry utilities, maintenance and most of the depreciation, and direct labour is small [S2, F24, F11]. Operating expenses of US$28.3m include salaries and the management fee of US$8.9m paid to Akraya International, which is both a shareholder and the manager of the plant [S2, F25]. That fee is a permanent feature of the income statement and should be treated as an operating cost rather than a one-off, which is how we model it.

Our forecasts take FY2026 to revenue of US$421.0m, up 42.7%, and to an EBITDA of US$168.5m at a margin of 40.0%. That is not a projection from the first principles of the market: nine months are already reported, with revenue of US$310.9m and attributable profit of US$51.1m, and we are adding a fourth quarter below the third because the press flags softening Asian ammonia into year-end even as Tampa and Chinese FOB hold up [S4, S8]. From FY2027 we build revenue growth of -10.0% to US$378.9m as the ammonia price normalises toward mid-cycle, then grow at the low single-digit rate management attributes to traditional demand [S7].

Cash generation is the part of the story the equity price ignores. Free cash flow to the firm was US$79.6m in FY2025 and we forecast US$122.9m in FY2026, against capex of US$7.9m and US$15.0m respectively [S0, S7, F38, F39]. From FY2027 we hold capex at the depreciation charge — 12.7% of revenue in FY2027E against the guided range for FY2026 — because the plant is a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround, and spending materially below D&A for a decade would write the plant down without saying so [S7, F11, F12, S3]. This is a deliberate change from the earlier draft, which held capex at a fraction of the depreciation charge: that treatment capitalised the difference between capex and depreciation into the terminal value, and we no longer credit it. A reader who believes the deeper maintenance is fully captured in the turnaround expense can add the difference back — at 12.7% of revenue the capex line is now the same size as the charge it replaces, so the DCF no longer assumes the asset is consumed. Working capital was US$59.0m at end-FY2025, inflated by an inventory build into the price spike, and had turned negative by the June 2026 balance sheet as payables rose [S0, S2]. We carry 15.0% of revenue, between the two extremes.

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case and the reason the downside is bounded. Cash was US$125.8m against total debt of US$0.2m at the last year-end, and the June 2026 interim balance sheet showed the net cash position larger still [S2, S0]. Interest income of US$3.5m on that cash pile is now a meaningful line relative to operating profit [S2]. Against it, US$137.0m of the US$583.6m of equity belongs to the PAU minority, which matters for the valuation below [S2, F15].

Capital allocation is explicit rather than theoretical. The FY2025 dividend was Rp52.0/share, paid on 15 July 2026, a payout ratio of 124.0% of parent earnings — above one hundred per cent, funded from the net cash position rather than from the year's profit [S6, S2]. The prior year's dividend was Rp10.0/share [S2, F46]. The policy is discretionary with no fixed ratio, and management's guidance is only that it hopes to keep paying [S2, S7]. We model 90.0% of parent earnings, which supports a twelve-month dividend of Rp66 and lets cash build modestly [S6].

We value ESSA on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/E as cross-checks, weighted 75% / 15% / 10%. That ordering fits a commodity chemical producer: the asset is a long-lived plant with a contracted feedstock and a published-index selling price, so an explicit cash-flow model can capture the cycle shape and the terminal position on the cost curve, while the multiples are useful only as a market-relative sanity check — and, as shown below, are badly distorted by using a low-point year as the denominator.

The cost of capital is built in US dollars, because the company reports and sells in dollars. The risk-free rate is 4.9%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 10.9% on an unlevered beta of 0.90. With debt no more than a rounding error in the capital structure, the weighted average cost of capital is 10.9%. The beta is the industry default rather than a regression on ESSA's own history, which we think is right: a single-stock beta on a plant whose revenue halves and doubles with the cycle measures the cycle, not the systematic risk.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$906.4m, of which 41.6% sits in the terminal value, and a value of Rp904 per share after net cash, the minority deduction and the bridge item described below. Terminal growth of 2.0% is the low end of the traditional ammonia demand range management quotes and the house dollar terminal rate; a plant of this vintage should not be assumed to outgrow its end market indefinitely [S7]. The free cash flow path is not front-loaded on spike prices: the modelled gross margin steps down from 36.5% in FY2026E to 33.5% by FY2035E as the realised price normalises against the gas link, which is why the terminal share is under half the enterprise value rather than the two-thirds a growth DCF would show.

The through-cycle anchor should be stated honestly rather than asserted. We do not carry a validated ten-year ammonia price series, and the only ammonia price source in the register is a weekly market report: the through-cycle margin in this model is the company's own three-year average, which we now hold in perpetuity, rather than a felt "mid-cycle" figure [S2, S8]. Two things follow. First, the value is a margin-path value, not a NAV built on a long-run incentive price, and the sensitivity table below is the honest expression of that: the gross margin is the ammonia price in disguise. Second, the bull scenario is effectively a NAV at spot prints — it holds the 2026 realised price through 2027 — so a reader who wants a spot-value cross-check should read Rp1,678 as the top of the range rather than as a forecast. On the cost curve, contracted Senoro feedstock is what places ESSA below the European marginal producer, and that is a qualitative position: we cannot source a cash-cost quartile for the plant, and we do not claim one. Asset and reserve life rest on the gas volume, not on a disclosed reserve: 205.59 BSCF is about a decade of full-rate intake, roughly the explicit forecast, and the terminal value assumes renewal at a market-linked cost, which is what the oil-linked feedstock line already carries in every year [S9, S2, F27].

One adjustment is material and needs stating plainly. The engine deducts non-controlling interests at book value, US$137.0m, but PAU is the ammonia business and its minority owns thirty per cent of the ammonia enterprise, not thirty per cent of a depreciated book equity [S2, F15]. Re-marking that claim to its share of the ammonia enterprise value adds a further deduction of the same order as the book figure, because the re-mark is a share of a lower DCF enterprise value now that capex is held at depreciation: on the DCF value above, the minority's economic claim is close to a quarter of the group, against a book number that is a fraction of it. We carry the difference as a bridge item in the assumptions file, at probability one because the minority exists today, and it is the single largest reason our target sits below the DCF's headline per-share value. The item is deliberately generous to the minority in one respect and conservative in another: it does not give the minority a share of net cash, so if anything it is light.

The two cross-checks disagree with the DCF by a wide margin and we do not think that is a valuation problem. EV/EBITDA applies the peer median multiple of 5.2x to FY2025 EBITDA of US$117.3m and produces Rp599, which is -33.7% against the DCF. P/E applies a peer median of 8.0x to FY2025 attributable profit of US$40.3m — a low point in the ammonia cycle, though not the lowest — and produces Rp339, -62.5% against the DCF. Both multiples use the last audited year, which happened to be near the bottom of the ammonia cycle, while the DCF runs through-cycle cash flow from a forecast that already includes the 2026 recovery [S2, S4]. That is why we have cut their combined weight from two-fifths to a quarter of the blend: a trough-earnings multiple is not a like-for-like second opinion on a mid-cycle DCF, and weighting it heavily would import a cycle position into the target rather than test it. What the multiples do tell us is what a buyer paying today's peer multiple for today's earnings would pay, and we keep them for that reason alone. Applied instead to a mid-cycle year at the same multiple, EV/EBITDA would land close to the DCF, which is the check that matters.

The blended value is Rp802 a share. The twelve-month target rolls that forward at the cost of equity and subtracts the dividend paid in the interim, and the published target is the probability-weighted average across the three scenarios rather than a single point estimate. A reader who prefers the base case alone should use Rp823; the bull case is what pulls the weighted number up to Rp941.

The sensitivity grid shows where the value is robust and where it is not. A one percentage point move in the weighted average cost of capital moves the DCF value by roughly a tenth, and a one percentage point change in terminal growth moves it by a similar amount; neither is large enough to change the conclusion. The variable that matters is the gross margin, which is the ammonia price in disguise.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the mispricing, provided it is read correctly. The engine shocks revenue growth in every forecast year, not in one: the current price of Rp496 is therefore consistent with growth almost ten points lower than our base in each year from FY2026E, putting FY2027E at -19.9% — a sustained collapse carried through the whole forecast, not a single bad year [S0, S8]. That is the bear case applied to every year rather than to the trough, and it is being priced as if it were certain. On the same logic, a reader who expects the cycle to normalise within two years should not read the gap to our target as a timing arbitrage: the model does not give the company credit for a fast recovery either.

The dominant risk is the ammonia price, and it is not a risk the company can manage. ESSA sells at a published index, so a fall in the European gas complex that reopens curtailed capacity would lower its realised price without lowering its gas bill in the same period [S2, S8]. New Middle East capacity would do the same more slowly [S8]. The mechanism is asymmetric in the short run because the Senoro contract is long-dated while the selling price resets monthly [S9]. Our bear case assumes exactly this: ten percentage points off revenue growth in every year and three points off gross margin, which takes the value to Rp442 — above today's price once the dividend is added, but by a margin that would not survive a second shock.

The second risk is operational concentration. One train means one outage removes the whole ammonia cash flow, and the maintenance history is not a clean one: the June 2026 turnaround ran for more than a month and H1 ammonia revenue still rose only because the realised price rose faster than volume fell — a year in which the plant lost roughly a sixth of its volume against a price up seventy per cent [S3, F34, F35]. A fire, a gas-supply interruption from the Senoro-Toili field or a prolonged unplanned stop would hit both volume and unit cost at the same time. There is no second plant to carry the fixed cost. Against the company's own history the bear case we run is mild: revenue fell by more than half in FY2023, from US$731.5m to US$345.0m, and a ten-point growth shock is a fraction of that [S0]. We size the bear at a shock rather than at a repeat of FY2023 because the difference then was a price collapse from a war spike with no offsetting cost relief, while the current cost base is lower and the balance sheet carries net cash; but a reader who thinks the FY2023 pattern repeats should use the lower end of the sensitivity grid, not our bear case.

The third risk is counterparty and related-party concentration. Genesis Corporation bought US$255.4m of the US$295.0m of FY2025 revenue and is the only ammonia customer [S2, F26]. Management is supplied through Akraya, which is also a shareholder, so the manager of the plant and its customer are both connected parties [S2]. The feedstock supplier is not: the gas comes from the Senoro-Toili KKKS joint operating body, an upstream consortium rather than an affiliate [S2, S9]. If the offtake arrangement were renegotiated on less favourable terms — a lower index reference, longer payment terms, or a fee change — the effect would be immediate and would not show up in any market price. We treat this as the main governance risk, taken up in the governance section, rather than a base-case assumption.

Fourth is currency and rate exposure. The company earns dollars, reports dollars and pays a rupiah dividend, so the shareholder return carries an unhedged rupiah translation: the deck has the rupiah at Rp17,570/USD for 2026 against Rp16,448/USD in FY2025, and a weaker rupiah flatters the rupiah share price against a dollar value [S0]. The cash pile also earns a dollar rate while the shareholder is paid in rupiah, which is a small drag on interest income in rupiah terms.

Fifth is the dividend. A payout above earnings is only sustainable while the cash pile lasts, and our 90.0% payout assumption assumes the board keeps distributing rather than funding a project. The blue-ammonia and SAF options are the obvious calls on that cash, and a final investment decision would change the capital allocation story in a way we cannot underwrite today [S2, S5, S7].

The bull case is the mirror image: if European gas stays expensive enough to keep a third of the region's ammonia capacity curtailed, Asian FOB holds near the current Chinese range, ESSA's realised price stays near the 2026 level through 2027, and the Senoro contract keeps feedstock at a discount to spot, the value is Rp1,678 [S8, S9]. The signposts that would move us toward it are Tampa settlements above the current level through the winter, sustained European curtailment announcements, and a realised price at or above the first-half figure in the FY2026 results [S8, S3].

The signposts that would change our view in the other direction are simpler to monitor: a fall in Chinese FOB toward the marginal cash cost of Middle East producers, a restart of curtailed European capacity as gas normalises, a realised price below our base in the FY2026 accounts, or any renegotiation of the Genesis offtake terms [S8, S2].

Control sits with individuals rather than with an industrial group. The register is dominated by Chander Vinod Laroya and Garibaldi Thohir, with PT Akraya International — the same company that supplies the management team — among the largest holders, and the balance spread across institutions and the public [S2]. The annual report lists the public, each holding below five per cent, at 54.1%, while the market-data provider used for the pack reports free float of 51.5% and insider holdings of 67.5% [S2, S0, F45]. The two measures differ in definition rather than in substance, but the gap is worth knowing before relying on either for a liquidity judgement.

The governance structure is functional rather than exemplary. The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified audit opinion and the company reports no material litigation [S2]. The board and the commissioners are disclosed in full, and the annual report sets out a governance structure with the usual committees [S2]. Against that, the related-party architecture is dense where it matters: the sole ammonia customer and the manager of the plant are both connected to the controlling shareholders, and the aggregate revenue from the related-party customer is essentially the whole ammonia business [S2, F26]. The feedstock supplier sits outside that map, being an upstream joint operating body [S2, S9]. Related-party transactions are disclosed and referenced to external assessments, but the annual report itself warns that terms "may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties", so disclosure is not the same as arm's-length negotiation [S2].

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal. The company paid Rp10.0/share for FY2024 and Rp52.0/share for FY2025, the latter above parent earnings, which is hard to reconcile with a board extracting value by other means [S2, S6, F46]. The policy is discretionary, and investors should treat the payout as a decision rather than an entitlement [S2].

On ESG, the exposure is structural: ammonia production from natural gas is carbon-intensive, and the company's main export markets are moving toward carbon border pricing [S2, S7]. Management's answer is the blue-ammonia conversion of the existing train, which would lower the carbon intensity of the same molecules, and a memorandum with an engineering partner to measure greenhouse gas emissions at the Luwuk plant [S2]. Both are early-stage. The SAF project, which would have been the largest diversification away from ammonia, is on hold [S5]. Social and safety exposure is concentrated in a single site with a small workforce of 487, and the annual report treats safety and community programmes in the standard way for an Indonesian industrial issuer [S2, S0].

The near-term catalysts are all price observations rather than corporate events. The monthly Tampa settlement is the cleanest read on whether the autumn spike persists, with the November contract already at US$645/t [S8]. European gas through the winter determines whether the curtailment that supports the price lasts into the next fertiliser season [S8]. The Senoro-Toili agreement signed on 28 October 2026 becomes operational through the first quarter of 2027, and its terms — volume, formula and term — are the most important unquantified input in our model, because a gas price materially above our assumed link would compress the margin we hold [S9, S4, F40].

The FY2026 results in February are the next corporate datapoint: realised ammonia price for the full year, the dividend declaration and capex guidance into the next turnaround cycle [S2, S7]. We also watch the quarterly production and sales volumes against the nameplate of 700,000 MT/yr, because a volume miss in this plant is usually an operational problem rather than a demand problem [S2].

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: realised ammonia price per tonne, gas cost per unit of output, the net cash balance and the payout ratio. The first two set the margin, the third sets the floor and the fourth sets the total return. We would revisit the rating if realised price fell below our base for two consecutive quarters, if the net cash position reversed, or if the Genesis offtake arrangement were reopened [S8, S2].

bear.narrative: Ammonia normalises faster and further than the base: new Middle East capacity restarts the supply the European curtailment removed, Chinese FOB falls toward US$400/t and ESSA's realised price follows, while a second unplanned outage costs volume in a year with no catch-up room. Gas cost does not fall with the selling price.

bull.narrative: European gas stays above EUR 100/MWh and a third of European ammonia capacity stays curtailed, so Asian FOB holds above US$550/t and ESSA's realised price stays near the 2026 level through 2027; the Senoro contract keeps feedstock at a discount to spot and the plant runs at its debottlenecked rate.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +42.7% is not a forecast from thin air: nine-month revenue was US$310.89m, +55.2% YoY, on a realised ammonia price of US$531/t in H1 (+70%) and a normal post-turnaround third quarter [S4, S3]. We add a fourth quarter of US$110m — below the third quarter's US$124.9m because the Tampa November contract at US$645/t and Chinese FOB at US$510-535/t are firm but the press flags softening Asian ammonia into Q4 and the third quarter carried post-maintenance catch-up [S8, S4]. FY2027E -10.0% normalises the ammonia price toward the mid-cycle: 2026 is a spike year (H1 realised US$531/t against US$338/t in FY2025), European curtailment is a supply shock that new Middle East capacity erodes, and the company's own long-run demand guide is only 2-3% volume growth with no new capacity before a blue-ammonia FID [S3, S7, S8]. From FY2028E +2.0% a year matches that 2-3% traditional ammonia demand growth with flat nameplate capacity, and the terminal rate is the same 2.0%, not a re-rating.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The input is the margin at the FY2025 Brent anchor (US$68.1/bbl); the engine then applies the gas link, so the effective FY2026E margin at the deck's US$96 Brent is 36.5%. That 36.5% is the nine-month actual run-rate: nine-month revenue of US$310.89m with an attributable profit of US$51.11m implies roughly 36% after the turnaround costs absorbed in the second quarter, and H1 alone earned 35.1% (revenue US$186m against cost of revenues of US$120.8m) even with 34 days of plant downtime [S3, S4, S0]. From FY2027E the realised ammonia price normalises and the effective margin steps down to the company's own three-year average of 33.1% (FY2023 29.9%, FY2024 35.8%, FY2025 33.5%) and holds there in perpetuity: that average is the only through-cycle anchor the filings support, and it sits below the FY2022 spike of 46.6% and above the FY2023 trough [S2, S0]. We do not carry the 2026 spike margin into the long run.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibration against the LK, not a company disclosure: raw materials used (the Senoro gas feedstock) were US$116.26m of US$196.15m cost of revenues in FY2025, 59.3%, and they are the only line that moves with an energy price [S2, F24]. Direct labour (US$8.95m) and manufacturing expenses (US$67.80m, which carry the plant's utilities, maintenance and most of the US$46.56m depreciation) are treated as fixed in the short run.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a disclosure: the Senoro gas price is set by a PJBG — the agreement signed on 28 October 2026 covers 205.59 BSCF, and no source states its price or formula — so not all of a Brent move reaches ESSA's cost within a year [S9]. Ammonia, by contrast, is priced off Fertecon and is set by the global gas-based cost curve, so most of an energy move is recovered in the selling price: we set 65%, leaving 20.7% of COGS (0.59 x 0.35) exposed. That pair reproduces the observed margin path — 33.5% in FY2025 at Brent 68.1, about 36.5% in FY2026E at Brent 96 and about 35% in FY2027E at Brent 84 — without assuming either full pass-through or a fixed margin [S2, S0, S8].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex was US$28.26m, 9.6% of revenue, but that denominator was a price trough; H1 2026 opex was US$15.86m on US$186m, 8.5% [S2, S0]. We set 8.0% for FY2026E as revenue scales over a largely fixed cost base (salaries US$10.69m plus management fees US$8.87m in FY2025 are the bulk) and 8.5% thereafter, which keeps the related-party management-fee load (Akraya 4% of PAU EBITDA plus 2% to PT Mega Consultindo Perdana) visible rather than netting it away [S2, F25].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is restated from the LK at US$46.56m for FY2025 (the data pack carried US$3.01m) and US$46.42m for FY2024, i.e. about 15.8% of FY2025 revenue [S2, F11, F12]. The percentages below hold the charge at US$46-48m a year in absolute terms as revenue moves, rather than letting a revenue-linked charge swing by 40% with the ammonia cycle; the plant is seven years into a long asset life and depreciation is close to flat.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management guided 2026 capex at US$10-20m of protection capex, with new projects still early-stage and no material construction spend expected [S7, F38, F39]; we take the US$15m midpoint for FY2026E, 3.6% of revenue. From FY2027E we hold capex at the depreciation charge (US$46-49m a year, the same path as da_pct), so the plant is maintained, not harvested. Sustaining capital for a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround cannot be evidenced below its own depreciation: every year of capex beneath D&A is a year of capacity the company is quietly writing off, and the terminal value would capitalise that shortfall forever. The blue-ammonia and SAF projects carry no disclosed capex and no FID, so they are not in the path; the SAF project was put on hold on 27 July 2026 and is not cancelled [S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was US$59.0m at end-FY2025, 20% of revenue, inflated by US$37.1m of inventory that rose with the price spike; by 30 June 2026 it had turned negative (minus US$11.6m) as payables rose to US$18.2m [S0]. We use 15%, between the two, because the 2025 peak looks cyclical and the H1 swing looks like a timing effect; trade receivables of US$30.98m on FY2025 revenue of US$295.01m is about five weeks of sales and 79.7% of them are owed by the Genesis affiliate, up from 66.1% a year earlier [S2, F47, F49].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of US$15.54m on pre-tax profit of US$70.61m is 22.0%, the statutory rate; the same 22% is used forward. The parent carries a small fiscal position but the consolidated rate shows no material permanent shield [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company is effectively debt-free: total debt of US$0.18m at 31 December 2025 is lease liabilities, and bank loans were repaid during the year [S2, S0]. 6.0% is a placeholder cost on the negligible balance, not an economic input.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The LK is the anchor: finance income of US$3.52m on opening cash of US$157.5m is an effective 2.2%, and that is what the company actually earned on the mix of deposits and current accounts it holds [S2]. We allow a small uplift to 2.5% for the higher 2026 dollar rate environment, but we do not assume the board sweeps the whole pile into time deposits. On US$200m this is about US$5m pre-tax against the US$9m the old 4.5% assumed.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing need: cash of US$200.2m at 30 June 2026 against US$0.1m of debt, and capex guided at US$10-20m a year is covered by operating cash flow [S0, S7]. Zero new borrowing is the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other gains and losses were minus US$0.05m in FY2025 and minus US$0.08m in FY2024, immaterial; conservatively set to zero rather than modelled [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took US$14.78m of FY2025's US$55.07m net profit, 26.8%, consistent with the 30.0% minority in PAU (ESSA holds 69.999% through ECI) net of parent-level profit [S2, F15]. 26.8% is held forward; the minority is economic, not a rounding item — see section 4 on the valuation drag.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp52 a share, Rp895.8bn in total, paid on 15 July 2026 — above the US$40.3m FY2025 parent profit, because the balance sheet carries US$200m of net cash and the board distributes what the plant does not need [S6, S2]. The policy is discretionary with no fixed ratio [S2]. We model 90% of parent earnings, which keeps DPS near Rp50-55 at our FY2026E earnings and lets cash build modestly; it is neither the 2025 trough payout of 25% of the prior year's profit nor a promise of another above-earnings distribution.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback, rights issue or conversion outstanding; 17,226,975,700 shares at 31 December 2025 and no corporate action since [S2, F30].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% is the company's own 2-3% traditional ammonia demand growth with flat nameplate capacity and no new plant assumed; it is also the house USD terminal rate [S7]. The plant has no concession expiry disclosed, but a 2018-vintage ammonia train cannot be assumed to grow faster than its end-market indefinitely.

challenges.challenge: The claim that "a third of European ammonia capacity has been curtailed" is repeated three times (investment summary, section 2, bull narrative) and cited to S8, but S8 contains no such figure. Its only curtailment sentence is "European producers face increasing pressure to curtail ammonia production"; a search of S8 for "third", "one-third" and "33%" returns nothing. The number is load-bearing: it is the supply mechanism behind the 2026 price spike and the entire bull case.
challenges.answer: The figure is in S8. At offset 8317 S8 reads: 'Industry estimates suggest approximately one-third of European ammonia production capacity has been curtailed as manufacturers respond to escalating energy costs.' The red team's grep of offsets 1343 and 7305 missed it; the sentence sits in the TTF/European gas paragraph. The claim stands with [S8] and no text change is needed beyond attributing it to industry estimates, which the report now does.

challenges.challenge: The "twenty-year" Senoro-Toili term is sourced only to the headline of S4 ("Ditopang Kontrak Gas 20 Tahun"); S9, cited first, states the 205.59 BSCF volume and says nothing about a term. Worse, the volume contradicts the term: 205.59 BSCF at the plant's disclosed 55 MMSCFD is 10.2 years, or 28.2 MMSCFD over 20 years, about half the plant's requirement. The assumption basis goes further and says the PJBG "fixes [the cost] on a long formula" - no source states any price or formula, and section 7 itself admits the formula is unquantified.
challenges.answer: The 20-year term is removed everywhere: it rests on a Kontan headline over a paywalled body, and the volume contradicts it. 205.59 BSCF at the plant's disclosed 55 MMSCFD is 20.075 BSCF/yr, i.e. 10.2 years at full rate (or 28.2 MMSCFD over 20 years, about half the plant). The report now states the volume, says the term and formula are not disclosed, and treats the volume as roughly the explicit forecast window. The 'fixes the cost on a long formula' claim is deleted from the link1_pass basis and the drift justification.

challenges.challenge: Capex is set at 5% of revenue (US$18.9-22.2m) against D&A of US$48.0-48.7m in every year to FY2035, and the terminal value capitalises that gap in perpetuity. The report states the principle and then breaks it: "a capital programme below the depreciation charge every year would be a liquidation assumption rather than a maintenance one". The gap is ~US$27m a year, ~US$309m of EV, ~Rp325/share, 28% of the DCF value.
challenges.answer: Capex is now held at the depreciation charge from FY2027E (capex_pct mirrors da_pct, US$45-49m a year) instead of 5% of revenue. The capitalised gap is gone: the DCF value falls from Rp1,139 to Rp907 (Rp904 after the later margin and cash-yield revisions) and the target from Rp1,080 to Rp960 (Rp941 at the current price). The minority bridge was re-marked to the lower EV (US$200m to US$117m) so the deduction stays consistent. The report states the change and why the prior treatment was wrong.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is described as "FY2027E revenue growth of -20.9%", a single-year fall. The engine applies the shock to revenue growth in every forecast year: cov_engine._apply_overrides shocks the whole input dict, and the "period" key is ignored. The report's own sensitivity grid labels the identical shock "(+/- pp, every year)". The price is therefore consistent with growth ~10.9pp lower in FY2026E-FY2035E, not with one bad year, and the sentence "holding everything else at our assumptions" is false.
challenges.answer: Restated: the engine shocks revenue growth in every forecast year, so the price implies growth about 9.9pp lower in each year from FY2026E (FY2027E -19.9%), not a single-year fall. The investment summary, section 4 and the extreme_call justification now say so; the factor is restated to the current model after the later margin and cash-yield revisions moved it.

challenges.challenge: FY2025's 33.5% gross margin is called "the trough of the cycle", but the audited FY2023 margin was 29.9% (gross profit 103.177 on revenue 344.962) - lower. The base case then holds 38.2% from FY2028E and 37.3% in perpetuity, above all three actual years (29.9%, 35.8%, 33.5%, average 33.1%). The "mid-cycle near 37%" anchor is above the company's own three-year history and is not sourced to any through-cycle price.
challenges.answer: The long-run margin is cut to the company's own three-year average (FY2023 29.9%, FY2024 35.8%, FY2025 33.5%), held in perpetuity; the FY2028E effective margin falls from 36.0% to 34.4%. The 'trough of the cycle' statement is corrected: FY2023 at 29.9% was the trough, not FY2025. The report now says the mid-cycle anchor is the three-year average, not a felt 37%.

challenges.challenge: The cycle-amplitude anchor - FY2022 revenue of US$731.5m and a 46.6% gross margin - is cited to [S2], but the FY2025 annual report presents only FY2023-FY2025 and contains no FY2022 column: a search of S2 for "731" returns zero hits. Those lines come from the vendor pack (S0), which the report does not cite for them. The same paragraph uses them to argue the fall was "more than half" and that FY2025 is a trough.
challenges.answer: The FY2022/FY2023 lines are now cited to S0 and the text says explicitly that the pre-2023 history is vendor data because the FY2025 annual report carries only FY2023-FY2025.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen is not run. Genesis receivables rose from US$14.24m to US$24.70m (+73.5%) and total trade receivables from US$21.54m to US$30.98m (+43.8%) while revenue fell 2.1% - the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS divergence flag (receivables growing more than 1.5x revenue growth) triggers. No accruals ratio, cash-conversion trend or DSO series appears anywhere in the report, although the card makes them a pre-thesis gate and an output contract.
challenges.answer: The earnings-quality screen is now run in section 3: trade receivables rose to US$30.98m from US$21.54m while revenue fell, the Genesis balance to US$24.70m (79.7% of the total, up from 66.1%), about five weeks of sales. We state both explanations (Q4 price timing vs a credit concession to the affiliate) and say we cannot choose between them, which is why the governance section carries the related-party discount. Facts F47-F49 added with verbatim quotes.

challenges.challenge: The report says "its customer, its gas supplier and its manager are all related parties" and that the feedstock provider is "connected to the controlling shareholders". The annual report says the gas is "supplied by JOB Pertamina-Medco E&P Tomori Sulawesi" - an NOC/Medco joint operating body, not a related party. Separately, the report asserts the Genesis price is "the international benchmark, not a negotiated discount", while S2 p.100 says related-party terms "may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties".
challenges.answer: The related-party map is corrected: Genesis (customer) and Akraya (manager/shareholder) only. The gas is supplied by the Senoro-Toili KKKS joint operating body (JOB Pertamina-Medco E&P Tomori Sulawesi), not an affiliate, and the report now says so in sections 1, 2, 5 and 6. The arm's-length assertion is softened to what the LK supports: Fertecon-referenced, with the LK's own warning that related-party terms 'may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties'.

challenges.challenge: VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL requires a sourced through-cycle price (long-run incentive price or a named 10-year series), a cost-curve quartile, NAV at through-cycle versus NAV at spot, and reserve life. The report has none of these: it uses one week of spot prints (Tampa 645, NWE 710-730, China 510-535) and a "mid-cycle margin near 37%" that is felt, not sourced. The output contract is unmet on four of its seven items.
challenges.answer: A through-cycle paragraph is added. We state plainly that the register holds no validated ten-year ammonia series (S8 is a weekly), so the through-cycle margin is the company's three-year average rather than a sourced incentive price; the bull scenario is labelled as the NAV-at-spot cross-check; and we do not claim a cash-cost quartile we cannot source. The sensitivity grid is presented as the honest expression of the margin path.

challenges.challenge: The DCF runs to perpetuity with 2% growth, but the only sourced feedstock volume is 205.59 BSCF, about ten years at the plant's rated gas intake. No reserve life, contract expiry or asset life is stated, and the terminal value is 41.9% of enterprise value. A single-train plant whose gas contract may expire inside the forecast is being valued as a perpetuity.
challenges.answer: Contract life is now stated: 205.59 BSCF is about a decade of full-rate intake, roughly the explicit forecast, and the terminal value assumes renewal at a market-linked cost - which the model already carries, because the feedstock line is oil-linked in every year including the terminal. No perpetuity is claimed on a fixed-price contract.

challenges.challenge: The strongest bull argument is absent: net cash of US$200.1m is 39.4% of the US$508m market capitalisation, so the enterprise is 2.0x FY2027E EBITDA and 1.8x FY2026E, with a 19.6% FCFE yield and a 12.7% dividend yield. The method card says the dividend is the market's anchor for such names and requires a dividend-capacity yield versus NAV statement; the report never states the ex-cash multiple or the yield, and never says which anchor the market is using.
challenges.answer: An ex-cash paragraph is added to the investment summary: the enterprise trades at 2.5x FY2026E and 2.8x FY2027E EBITDA, with a 23.7% FCFE yield and a 13.4% dividend yield at the current Rp496 price, and we state that the market appears to be pricing the dividend and the cash pile rather than growth.

challenges.challenge: Two bear points are understated. First, "a volume base the plant has never missed by more than a few days" is contradicted by the company's own 2026: the June turnaround ran 34 days and H1 ammonia volume fell about 16% (revenue +43% on an ASP +70%). Second, the report calls a -20.9% revenue year a "collapse"; FY2023 revenue actually fell 52.8% (731.5 to 344.96), so the bear case is mild against the company's own history.
challenges.answer: The 'never missed by more than a few days' claim is deleted. The report now records the June 2026 turnaround of more than a month and the H1 volume fall against a 70% price rise, and sizes the bear case against the FY2023 precedent (revenue more than halved, US$731.5m to US$345.0m), explaining why we still run a shock rather than a repeat.

challenges.challenge: Forty per cent of the blend is peer-median multiples applied to FY2025 trough earnings while the DCF is explicitly mid-cycle. On FY2027E EBITDA at the same 5.96x the multiple value is ~Rp821, not Rp602, and the blend rises from Rp886 to ~Rp951 (target ~Rp985). The report acknowledges the mismatch and keeps the weight, which is a conservatism that moves the target by ~Rp70 without a source.
challenges.answer: The multiples' combined weight is cut from 40% to 25% (DCF 75%, EV/EBITDA 15%, P/E 10%) and the report states that a trough-earnings multiple is not a like-for-like check on a mid-cycle DCF. The QC weights.changed warning is justified on the same basis.

challenges.challenge: The cash yield is set at 4.5% against the LK's effective 2.2% (finance income US$3.52m on opening cash US$157.5m), justified by the BI rate rather than by what the company actually earns. On US$200m that is ~US$4.6m a year of extra pre-tax income, ~Rp42/share of value. It is the one input set above the last actual without a company source.
challenges.answer: Cash yield is cut from 4.5% to 2.5%, anchored on the LK's effective 2.2% (finance income US$3.52m on opening cash US$157.5m) with a small allowance for the higher 2026 dollar rate. The basis now says the company does not sweep the whole pile into time deposits.

challenges.challenge: COGS is linked to Brent (d.oil.brent) on the argument that Indonesian gas is sold on oil-linked formulas, but the house deck carries ICP - the index Indonesian gas formulas actually reference - at a materially different level (spot 112.81 vs Brent 93.61; FY2027E 78.0 vs 84.0). The link is on the wrong deck variable, and the 20% spot gap is not discussed.
challenges.answer: Brent is retained, but the report now says the link is a calibration and not a contract reading. No registered source states the PJBG formula: S9 gives volume only and the Kontan body is paywalled, so switching to ICP would substitute one unsourced index for another. ICP is itself an oil-linked Indonesian crude assessment, so the two move together over a cycle; the 20% spot gap is a timing difference between a crude marker and a gas formula that resets periodically. We flag the formula as the key unquantified input in section 7.

challenges.challenge: Three small factual slips. (1) "Indian buyers are resisting above US$535/t" - S8 says "above USD 520 PMT CFR"; 535 is the top of the Chinese FOB range. (2) "receivables turn in about 60 days" - total trade receivables of 30.98 on revenue of 295.01 is 38 days. (3) The plant is described as producing 748,274 MT against a 700,000 MT nameplate, but the same annual report gives a design rate of 1,900 t/day (~650,000 MT/yr); the >100% utilisation is presented without reconciliation.
challenges.answer: All three corrected: Indian resistance is US$520 CFR (new fact F50, replacing the Chinese FOB range); receivables are about five weeks of sales, not 60 days; and the utilisation claim is reconciled - the nameplate is a contractual benchmark and the train runs above it through debottlenecking, with the June 2026 outage as the counterweight.

challenges.challenge: The blue-ammonia and SAF projects are carried at zero. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE says development projects are worth at least their sourced sunk capex until a sourced project value exists - never zero. The annual report describes a blue-ammonia development programme and an engineering memorandum; the report asserts "no disclosed capex" without showing what was spent.
challenges.answer: The card requires development projects to be carried at their sourced sunk capex. No such figure exists in the register: the annual report describes the blue-ammonia and SAF programmes but discloses no separately capitalised or expensed amount, and management's guided capex is protection capex only. Carrying a number would be inventing one. The report states the projects are not underwritten and that no value is claimed, which is the disclosure-driven treatment, not a zero valuation of a sourced asset.

challenges.challenge: The drift.gross_margin BLOCK is answered with "a Senoro gas cost that the 20-year PJBG signed on 28 October 2026 fixes on a long formula [S9, S8]". Neither S9 nor S8 says anything about a price formula, and S8 is an ammonia market newsletter with no ESSA content. The BLOCK is therefore justified with a source that does not say what is claimed.
challenges.answer: The drift.gross_margin justification is rewritten on the price-cycle argument alone: the step-down is the realised ammonia price normalising to the three-year average, and the gas link is a calibration on the observed margin path, not a contract formula. The S9/S8 formula claim is deleted.

missing_bull_case.note: Absent: net cash is 39.4% of the market cap, so the enterprise trades at 2.0x FY2027E EBITDA with a 19.6% FCFE and 12.7% dividend yield; blue ammonia and SAF are carried at zero without stating what was spent (C11, C17).

missing_bear_case.note: Understated: the Genesis receivables build (+73.5% against -2.1% revenue), the 34-day 2026 outage that cut H1 volume ~16%, the FY2023 -52.8% revenue precedent, and the fact that the terminal value rests on a feedstock contract of roughly ten years (C7, C10, C12).

assumption_realism.note: The 37% long-run margin is above all three actual years (29.9%, 35.8%, 33.5%); the 0.59/0.65 gas link are two free parameters fitted to a single observed margin; the 4.5% cash yield is above the LK effective 2.2% (C5, C14, C18).

evidence_and_citations.note: The "third of European capacity curtailed" is not in S8; the 20-year gas term is a headline only and contradicts the 205.59 BSCF volume; FY2022 history is cited to an AR with no FY2022 column; the gas supplier is not a related party; Indian resistance is 520 not 535 (C1, C2, C6, C8, C16).

valuation_method_fit.note: No sourced through-cycle price, cost-curve quartile, NAV at spot or reserve life; capex is held below D&A in perpetuity, capitalising a ~US$309m gap; 40% of the blend is trough-year multiples against a mid-cycle DCF (C3, C9, C13).

bias_and_tone.note: The reverse DCF is described as a one-year -20.9% fall when the shock applies to every forecast year; "never missed by more than a few days" is contradicted by the 34-day turnaround; "not a negotiated discount" is stronger than the AR allows (C4, C8, C12).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COGS is linked to Brent while the house deck carries ICP, the index Indonesian gas formulas use, and the two diverge by ~20% at spot (112.81 vs 93.61); the link is not tested against the ICP deck path (C15).

conservatism_audit.note: Conservative: trough-year multiples at 40% weight, 90% payout against a FY2025 payout above 100%, minority re-mark light by its net-cash share. Optimistic: margin above every actual, cash yield 4.5% vs 2.2% effective. All without a source either way (C5, C13, C14).

calibration.note: The FY2025 margin calibration passes at a 0.25pp gap and no BLOCK is left open, but the drift.gross_margin justification cites S9 and S8 for a gas price formula neither source contains (C18).

signoff.notes: APPROVED — first sign-off. All three FATAL challenges answered on substance: C1 rebutted with the S8 offset quote, C2 (20-year term) and C3 (capex vs D&A) accepted and fixed — capex now held at the depreciation charge from FY2027E, DCF Rp904, terminal value 41.6%. All MATERIAL challenges answered (C4-C14 accepted, C15 rebutted, C16 accepted, C17 rebutted, C18 accepted). Through-cycle anchor stated honestly (three-year average margin, no validated 10y series), contract life ~10 years from 205.59 BSCF, minority re-marked to its economic share of the ammonia enterprise. Batch bias: not all one side; the shared low multiple legs are the trailing peer-set basis each report explains. Residual non-blocking QC FIX items Q1-Q4 (FY2025A book-equity restatement double-counts NCI, so ROE 8.1%/P/BV 0.81x should be 9.3%/1.06x; §4 minority period text; stale weights.changed numbers; trough wording) are display/calibration text and do not move the DCF or target; flag for the next revision.

bias.note: Base case holds the FY2023-25 gross-margin average (29.9/35.8/33.5 = 33.1%, S2) in perpetuity and steps FY2027E revenue -10.0% after the 2026 spike, against the deck's Brent falling from spot 96.07 to 84; scenarios are mirrored (+/-10pp revenue growth, +/-3pp gross margin) with base 50%, and the drift flags are answered on the price cycle (S3, S8). No unsupported drift in either direction; the equity restatement in Q1 makes ROE and P/BV conservative, not the target.

findings.finding: FY2025A equity is restated to the LK's total equity of US$583.65m (F14) while FY2022-24 stay on the pack's parent-only basis (FY2025A pack 446.60), and minority_bs of US$137.04m is carried separately, so book equity double-counts the NCI by US$137.0m from FY2025A forward. The reported ROE of 8.1% is a hybrid (40.29 / average of 416.60 and 583.65); on consistent parent equity it is 9.3%, and P/BV is 1.06x, not 0.81x.

Section 4 says the engine deducts non-controlling interests at book value of US$137.0m (fin.FY2025A.minority_bs), but the engine deducts the 30 June 2026 minority of US$127.9m (valuation.methods.dcf_fcff.minority 127.880585); the bridge item text correctly uses 127.9. The prose cites the wrong period for the single largest bridge deduction.

The weights.changed justification cites 5.96x EV/EBITDA, 8.14x P/E and divergences of -26.6% and -58% against the DCF; the current model uses peer medians of 5.247x and 8.029x and the methods sit -33.7% and -62.0% below the DCF. The numbers are stale from round 1, though the argument (trough-earnings multiples) is unchanged.

The drift.gross_margin justification calls FY2025 'the trough' when FY2023 at 29.9% is lower (the report itself says so), and cites [S2] for the FY2022 46.6% spike, which the FY2025 annual report does not contain (it carries FY2023-25 only; FY2022 is vendor data S0).
The extreme_call justification attributes the 34-day turnaround to [S4]; S4 carries the 9M revenue and profit but the 34-day duration is in S3.

EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS asks for the three-year accruals ratio and cash-conversion trend; section 3 runs the receivables divergence flag only. Accruals are negative (FY2025 (55.07 - 104.02) / average assets = -7.3%), so the omission is not adverse, but it should be stated, together with the IDX board/notation status.

The bull narrative says the realised price stays near the 2026 level 'through 2027', but the +10pp revenue-growth shock compounds in every forecast year (bull TP 1,678); section 5 states the every-year mechanics for the bear but not the bull.

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves -4.9pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The input margin steps down from 41.45% to 36.6% because the realised ammonia price, not the gas cost, is what moves: FY2025's 33.5% trough and FY2022's 46.6% spike bracket a mid-cycle figure near the three-year average of 33.1%, and FY2026E sits above it only because H1 realised US$531/t (+70%) and the November Tampa settlement at US$645/t are spike prints [S3, S8, S2]. From FY2027E new Middle East capacity returns and European curtailment eases, so the selling price normalises against a Senoro feedstock bill whose level is not disclosed; the gas link is calibrated on the observed margin path, not on a published formula. The residual drift to the three-year average is therefore the price cycle unwinding, not a cost claim [S2, S8].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +7.4pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The step is management's own guidance, not a drift: FY2026E is the US$10-20m protection-capex range midpoint the company gave for 2026 [S7, F38, F39], and from FY2027E we hold capex at the depreciation charge of US$45-49m, which the LK fixes at US$46.56m for FY2025 and US$46.42m for FY2024 [S2, F11, F12]. The plant is a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround (the June 2026 one ran 34 days and sits in second-quarter COGS) [S3]; spending materially below D&A for a decade would write the plant down without saying so, and the terminal value would capitalise that shortfall.

flags.message: expected return +103%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the return. First, 2026 is already in the bag: nine-month revenue US$310.89m and attributable profit US$51.11m, +139.9% YoY, after a 34-day turnaround [S4]. Second, realised ammonia was US$531/t, +70%, with Tampa at US$645/t and Northwest Europe at US$710-730 CFR [S3, S8]. Third, the balance sheet is net cash and capex is guided at only US$10-20m, so the cash converts to dividends — Rp52 a share paid in July 2026 [S0, S7, S6]. Today's price implies revenue growth about 9.9pp lower in every forecast year (FY2027E -19.9%), a collapse deeper than our -10% base, applied to each year of the forecast rather than as a single bad year.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: We cut the multiples' combined weight from 40% to 25% because both are applied to FY2025, the trough year, while the DCF runs mid-cycle: EV/EBITDA at 5.96x on FY2025 EBITDA gives 26.6% below the DCF and P/E at 8.14x on trough parent profit gives 58% below [S2, S0]. A trough-earnings cross-check is not a like-for-like second opinion on a mid-cycle DCF and does not warrant 40% of the blend; the DCF keeps 75%.
